fields.Back: End-to-end resources (link capacity, buffers) are allocated to and reserved for a 'call' between source and destination for its duration; dedicated resources, no sharing, guaranteed circuit-like performance; used in traditional telephone networks.

fields.Front: In circuit switching, what happens to a circuit segment when the call is not using it?
fields.Back: It sits idle: no sharing, so reserved but unused capacity is wasted (e.g., silent periods in a phone call).

fields.Text: Circuit switching: resources are {{c1::reserved}} for the call, giving {{c2::guaranteed}} performance, but idle circuit capacity is {{c3::wasted (no sharing)}}; commonly used in {{c4::traditional telephone networks}}.
A circuit on a link is implemented with either {{c1::frequency division multiplexing (FDM)}} or {{c2::time division multiplexing (TDM)}}.

fields.Back: The link's optical/electromagnetic frequency range is divided into narrow frequency bands; each call gets its own band for the whole call and transmits at the max rate of that narrow band, all the time.
Time is divided into frames, each into slots; each call gets the same periodic slot(s) in every frame and may transmit at the max rate of the full (wider) band, but only during its slot.

fields.Text: FDM: each call gets its own narrow {{c1::frequency band}} all the time. TDM: each call gets the whole band only during its periodic {{c2::time slot(s)}}.

fields.Front: Numeric: a 1.536 Mbps TDM link has 24 slots. What is the rate of one circuit, and how long to send 640,000 bits if circuit setup takes 500 ms?
fields.Back: One circuit = 1.536 Mbps / 24 = 64 kbps. Transmission = 640,000 / 64,000 = 10 s. Total = 10 s + 0.5 s = 10.5 s (independent of number of links).

fields.Front: Slide example: 1 Gb/s link, each user needs 100 Mb/s when active and is active 10% of the time. How many users under circuit switching?
fields.Back: 1 Gb/s / 100 Mb/s = 10 users (100 Mb/s must be reserved per user at all times).

fields.Front: Slide example: same 1 Gb/s link with packet switching and 35 users. What is the probability that more than 10 users are active simultaneously, and how is it computed?
fields.Back: About 0.0004. It is the binomial tail: sum for k = 11..35 of C(35,k) (0.1)^k (0.9)^(35-k). So 35 users are served with essentially no delay 99.96% of the time.

fields.Text: In the 1 Gb/s example, circuit switching supports {{c1::10}} users while packet switching supports {{c2::35}} users with probability of more than 10 active being less than {{c3::0.0004}}.

fields.Front: What happens in the 35-user example if there are more than 35 users?
fields.Back: The probability that more than 10 are simultaneously active grows, so overload becomes common: queues build at the link, causing delay and packet loss.

fields.Front: Textbook example: 10 users share a 1 Mbps link; one user sends 1,000 packets of 1,000 bits while the others are idle. Time under TDM (10 slots) vs packet switching?
fields.Back: TDM: the user gets 1/10 of the link, so 1 Mbit takes 10 s. Packet switching: the user sends at the full 1 Mbps and finishes in 1 s.

fields.Front: Why is packet switching good for 'bursty' data?
fields.Back: Bursty sources sometimes have data and sometimes not; packet switching allocates link capacity on demand (resource sharing) and is simpler with no call setup, so idle capacity is used by others.

fields.Front: What is the main drawback of packet switching, and what does it require?
fields.Back: Excessive congestion is possible: packet delay and loss from buffer overflow. It requires protocols for reliable data transfer and congestion control.

fields.Text: Packet switching is great for {{c1::bursty}} data (resource sharing, no call setup) but suffers possible {{c2::congestion}} (delay and loss), requiring protocols for {{c3::reliable data transfer and congestion control}}.

fields.Front: Give the restaurant analogy for circuit vs packet switching.
fields.Back: Circuit switching = restaurant requiring reservations (hassle up front, guaranteed table). Packet switching = no reservations (no hassle, but you may have to wait for a table).
